documents.title: A museum rethinks what it means to own a masterpiece
documents.text:
The Hallam Museum's decision to lend its most celebrated painting to a rival institution for five years has provoked a surprising amount of anger among its own members. The work, a seventeenth-century interior by a Dutch master, has hung in the same room since 1921 and appears on the museum's posters, tote bags and annual report.

The director, Camille Reyes, defends the arrangement as a matter of arithmetic. The loan will bring in a sum equal to nearly a tenth of the annual budget, enough to repair the roof of the east wing, which has leaked for a decade. In return the Hallam will receive on loan a group of sculptures it could never afford to acquire. "A collection is not a vault," she said. "Its purpose is to be seen, and a picture that stays put is seen by fewer people than one that travels."

Critics find this reasoning too convenient. They note that the painting is the museum's chief attraction, and that visitor numbers are likely to fall once it has gone. Some members have threatened to cancel their subscriptions. Ms. Reyes concedes that she cannot rule out a decline, but she points out that two earlier lending programs, which were also controversial, ended with higher attendance than before. Whether the same will be true here depends, she admits, on how persuasive the replacement exhibition proves.

choices: The sale of a famous painting to a rival museum
The discovery of a lost seventeenth-century painting
A museum's debated loan of its best-known work
The closure of the museum's east wing for repairs
questions.explanation: The Hallam is lending its famous painting for five years, and members are upset.

choices: To mend the leaking roof of one wing
To buy sculptures from the rival institution
To lower the price of membership subscriptions
To print posters and annual reports
questions.explanation: The sum is enough to repair the roof of the east wing.

choices: The museum should lock away its best pieces

questions.explanation: She argues a collection's purpose 'is to be seen', and that traveling art reaches more people.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from her mention of two earlier programs?

She hopes attendance will rise despite the loss
Those programs lost a great deal of money
She is certain that visitor numbers will certainly grow
questions.explanation: She cannot rule out a decline but notes earlier controversial programs ended with higher attendance.

documents.title: Response to a supplier's late-delivery claim
documents.text:
To: Beatrix Lindqvist, Sales Manager, Norland Components
From: Ahmed Karimi, Procurement, Teverton Machines
Subject: Your claim regarding late delivery penalties

Dear Ms. Lindqvist,

Thank you for your email of 4 June, in which you say that we have no grounds to withhold the penalty clause from the contract. I have reviewed the correspondence with my colleagues and cannot accept that conclusion, though I agree that the matter is more nuanced than either of us would like.

You are correct that the delivery of the gearboxes arrived eleven days late, and that our contract specifies a penalty of one percent per week of delay. However, our records show that the delay began with your own warehouse, which did not ship the order until 20 May, a week after the confirmation date. Moreover, your email of 14 May, which I have attached, explicitly promised dispatch by 17 May. This, in our opinion, is a breach on your side, not a circumstance beyond your control.

I do not wish to turn a long relationship into a quarrel. If you can show that the warehouse delay was caused by a shipping disruption rather than a decision to prioritize another client, I will gladly reconsider. Otherwise, we shall deduct two percent from the June payment, as the contract permits.

Sincerely,
Ahmed Karimi

choices: To reject a supplier's argument on penalties
To order a much larger batch of gearboxes
To complain about the quality of the product
To confirm that a payment was received in full
questions.explanation: He refuses to accept Ms. Lindqvist's conclusion and says a penalty will be deducted.

choices: One week

questions.explanation: The gearboxes arrived eleven days late.

questions.explanation: The delay 'began with your own warehouse', which shipped a week after the confirmation date.

documents.title: Customer support chat: a billing dispute
documents.text:
Agent (Lucia) [14:03]: Thank you for contacting Veridian Mobile. How can I help?

Customer [14:04]: I was charged 79 dollars this month, but my plan is 49. I was told in March that the price was fixed for two years.

Lucia [14:06]: Let me look. I can see that a roaming charge of 30 dollars was added on the 11th, when your phone connected to a network in Morocco.

Customer [14:07]: I was never in Morocco. I was on a ferry, and I turned off data.

Lucia [14:09]: That would explain it. Ferries often carry their own mobile networks, which are billed as international roaming even in coastal waters. I'm afraid the charge is technically valid, because the network identified itself as foreign.

Customer [14:10]: That seems unfair. The contract says nothing about ferries.

Lucia [14:12]: I understand. I cannot remove the charge myself, but I can refer it to the disputes team, who have discretion in cases like this. You will hear from them within five working days, and the amount will be held while they decide.

Customer [14:13]: Fine. Please also add a note that I want a block on roaming in future.

Lucia [14:14]: Done. The block will take effect within the hour.

questions.explanation: The bill was 79 instead of 49 because of a 30-dollar roaming charge.

documents.title: The slow decline of the handwritten letter
documents.text:
Postal services across Europe report that the volume of personal letters has fallen by more than eighty percent in two decades. Yet the collapse is not as complete as the statistics suggest, because the letters that remain have changed character. Where once a letter carried news, it now carries meaning: condolences, apologies, thanks that the writer feels cannot be sent by message without seeming casual.

Researchers who interviewed two hundred regular letter writers found that most had adopted the habit deliberately, often after a period of illness or bereavement. "It is the slowness that matters," said one participant, a retired engineer. "A message says that you thought of someone in the last minute. A letter says that you set aside an hour for them." Several admitted that they write fewer letters than they once did, but expect each to be kept.

The economics of the postal service, however, remain grim. Delivering a single letter to an isolated address costs far more than the stamp, and governments are reluctant to subsidize a service that fewer households use. Some have proposed ending daily collection in favor of two or three deliveries a week. Writers, predictably, have objected, though a few concede that a slower post might even suit the form: a letter that arrives on Thursday is no worse for not having arrived on Tuesday.

choices: Postal services are growing in spite of email

questions.explanation: Volume has collapsed, but remaining letters carry meaning rather than news.

choices: It is cheaper and faster than any message

questions.explanation: 'A letter says that you set aside an hour for them.'

questions.explanation: Delivering to an isolated address 'costs far more than the stamp'.

choices: They want daily collection to continue unchanged

They might accept slower delivery calmly
They think that Tuesdays are the best days for mail
questions.explanation: A few concede that a slower post might suit the form.

documents.title: Notice of changes to the staff expense policy
documents.text:
NOTICE TO ALL EMPLOYEES
Effective 1 September, the company's travel and expense policy will change in three respects.

First, advance approval will be required for any hotel stay exceeding 180 dollars per night. Until now, employees could exceed this limit if they justified the cost afterwards; this flexibility has been withdrawn because the number of retrospective explanations has risen sharply and the finance team can no longer review them properly.

Second, meals during travel will be reimbursed up to a daily allowance of 65 dollars, replacing the previous system of itemized claims. Employees need no longer submit restaurant receipts, but they will be unable to claim more than the allowance, even in expensive cities. The company judges that the reduction in paperwork outweighs the occasional inconvenience.

Third, claims must be submitted within thirty days of the end of the trip. Claims received after this period will be paid only with the written consent of a department head, and no exception will be made for claims older than ninety days.

Questions should be sent to expenses@harbourtech.example. A summary sheet is available on the intranet.

documents.title: Letter to a shareholder concerning dividend policy
documents.text:
Dear Mr. Okonkwo-Hale,

Thank you for your letter of 2 February, in which you ask why the board has recommended a lower dividend this year, despite the company having reported its highest revenue on record. It is a fair question, and I should like to answer it directly.

The decision reflects the fact that revenue and profit are not the same thing. Our turnover grew by nine percent, but raw material costs rose by fourteen percent, and we absorbed most of that increase rather than passing it on to customers, many of whom operate on tight margins of their own. The result was a profit slightly below last year's. Distributing the same dividend would have meant drawing on reserves that we intend to use for the new plant in Gdańsk, whose cost has also risen.

I appreciate that this will disappoint shareholders who rely on the dividend as income. The board debated the matter at length, and the final vote was close. Should conditions improve, we expect to return to the previous level within two years, though I would be misleading you if I presented that as a promise.

I hope this clarifies our reasoning, and I should be happy to discuss it at the annual meeting.

Yours sincerely,
Eleanor Fairweather, Chair

questions.explanation: The chair explains why the board recommended a lower dividend.

questions.explanation: Turnover grew nine percent, but material costs rose fourteen percent.

documents.title: About the Fernhill Community Orchard
documents.text:
The Fernhill Community Orchard began in 2009 as a neglected patch of land behind the library, which the council had planned to sell for housing. A group of neighbors, led by a retired schoolteacher, persuaded the authorities to lease it for a nominal rent instead, and within three years had planted more than sixty trees.

Today, the orchard is run entirely by volunteers, and anyone may take part. We hold working days on the first Saturday of each month, when members prune, plant and repair the paths. No experience is necessary; the more skilled volunteers are happy to teach. In autumn, we invite residents to pick the fruit, and whatever is not eaten is pressed into juice that is sold at the market to pay for tools.

We should be honest about the difficulties. The lease expires in 2029, and although the council has said that it values the site, nothing has been guaranteed. A recent attack by canker disease killed eleven of our oldest trees, and replacing them will take years. We therefore welcome donations of any size, as well as offers of professional advice from anyone with experience in fruit-growing or in negotiating leases.

To join us, simply turn up on a working day. There are no fees and no forms.
